blocks.text: The same alternation is observed in keeping watch. For when, tired from flying, they come down to the ground to rest and sleep, while the rest sleep, one or two, or a few out of the whole number, keep watch in turn over the entire flock. Aristotle, book 9, ch. 10: Ὅταν δὲ καθίζωνται, αἱ μὲν ἄλλαι, ὑπὸ τῇ πτέρυγι τὴν κεφαλὴν ἔχουσαι, καθεύδουσιν ἐπὶ ἑνὸς ποδὸς ἐναλλάξ, ὁ δὲ ἡγεμὼν γυμνὴν ἔχων τὴν κεφαλὴν προορᾷ, καὶ ὅταν αἴσθηταί τι, σημαίνει βοῶν [Hotan de kathizōntai, hai men allai, hypo tē pterygi tēn kephalēn echousai, katheudousin epi henos podos enallax, ho de hēgemōn gymnēn echōn tēn kephalēn proora, kai hotan aisthētai ti, sēmainei boōn], When they settle, the others sleep with the head hidden under the wing, standing on one foot and then the other. But the leader (that is, the watchman) looks out with his head uncovered, and signals by his voice what he has perceived. Antigonus follows the same in the Mirabilia, ch. 46, and so does Alkazuinius with the Auctarium: واذا ارادت النوم ادخل كل واحد راسه تحت جناحها لعلمها ان الجناح احمل للصدمة من الراس لما فيه من العين التي هي اشرف الاعضا والدماغ الذي هو ملاك البدن ونام كل واحد منها قايما علي احدي رجليه حتي لا يكون نومها ثقيل واما قايدها وحارسها فلا ينام ولا يدخل راسه في جناحه ولا يزال ينظر من جميع الجوانب فان احس باحد صاح باعلا صوته فاخبر اصحابه بالعدو [wa-idhā arādat al-nawm adkhala kull wāḥid raʾsahu taḥt janāḥihā li-ʿilmihā anna al-janāḥ aḥmal li-l-ṣadma min al-raʾs li-mā fīhi min al-ʿayn allatī hiya ashraf al-aʿḍā wa-l-dimāgh alladhī huwa milāk al-badan wa-nāma kull wāḥid minhā qāyiman ʿalā iḥdā rijlayhi ḥattā lā yakūn nawmuhā thaqīl wa-ammā qāyiduhā wa-ḥārisuhā fa-lā yanām wa-lā yudkhil raʾsahu fī janāḥihi wa-lā yazāl yanẓur min jamīʿ al-jawānib fa-in aḥassa bi-aḥad ṣāḥa bi-aʿlā ṣawtihi fa-akhbara aṣḥābahu bi-l-ʿaduww] When they wish to sleep, they put their heads [II, 625] under their wings, because they know that the wings bear a blow better than the head, in which is the eye, the noblest of the parts, and the brain, on which the rest of the body depends. They sleep, moreover, standing on one foot, so that their sleep may not be heavy. But the one who is leader and guard abstains from sleep and does not hide his head under his wings. Rather, he continually looks out on every side. And if he perceives anyone, he cries out with a loud voice to signal to his companions that an enemy is near. Others add two further points. The first is that cranes keep watch in turn. Horus, book 2, ch. 90: Αὗται γὰρ ἑαυτὰς φυλάττουσι γρηγοροῦσαι κατ᾽ ὄρδινον ἐν πάσῃ τῇ νυκτί [Hautai gar heautas phylattousi grēgorousai kat᾽ ordinon en pasē tē nykti]. They guard themselves, keeping watch in order through the whole night. Solinus: They divide the night watches, so that every tenth one is sleepless. Isidore: At night they divide the watches, and keep the order of the vigils by turns. Cassiodorus: They watch in turn, and guard themselves by common caution. Basil: Τοῦ καιροῦ τῆς φυλακῆς πληρομένου, ἡ μὲν βοήσασα πρὸς ὕπνον ἐτράπετο. ἡ δὲ τὴν διαδοχὴν ὑποδεξαμένη, ἧς ἔτυχεν ἀσφαλείας, [col. 76] ἀντέδωκεν ἐν τῷ μέρει [Tou kairou tēs phylakēs plēromenou, hē men boēsasa pros hypnon etrapeto. hē de tēn diadochēn hypodexamenē, hēs etychen asphaleias, antedōken en tō merei]. Ambrose expands this as follows: When the time of the watch has been completed, having discharged its duty it settles down to sleep after first giving a cry, so as to wake the sleeper to whom it is to hand over its turn of duty. And that one willingly takes up its lot, and does not, as is our habit, renounce sleep unwillingly and sluggishly. Rather, it briskly shakes itself from its bed, performs its turn, and repays the favour it received with equal care and service. And Damir: في طبعه الخوف والتحارس بالنوبة فاذا قضي نوبتة قام الذي كان نايما يحرس مكانه حتي تقضي كله ما يلزمها من الحراسة [fī ṭabʿihi al-khawf wa-l-taḥārus bi-l-nawba fa-idhā qaḍā nawbatahu qāma alladhī kāna nāyiman yaḥrus makānahu ḥattā taqḍī kulluhu mā yalzamuhā min al-ḥirāsa] It is in its nature to be fearful and to keep guard by turns. And when one has completed its turn, one of those that were sleeping rises to keep watch in its place, until all have kept the watches incumbent on them. The second is that the watchmen carry a stone in the foot, which by its fall wakes them when asleep or about to fall asleep. Pliny: They keep watches at night, holding a pebble in the foot, which, loosened by sleep and falling, betrays their negligence. Solinus: The watchmen grasp small weights in their toes, which, if they should happen to fall, betray sleep. Plutarch: Αἱ προφυλακὴν ἔχουσαι νυκτὸς, ἐπὶ θατέρου σκέλους ὀχοῦνται τὸ σῶμα, τῷ δ᾽ ἑτέρῳ ποδὶ λίθον περιλαβοῦσαι κρατοῦσι· συνέχει γὰρ ὁ τῆς ἀφῆς τόνος ἐν τῷ μὴ καθεύδειν πολὺν χρόνον. Ὅταν δὲ ἀνῶσιν, ἐκπεσὼν ὁ λίθος ταχὺ διήγειρε τὴν προεμένην [Hai prophylakēn echousai nyktos, epi thaterou skelous ochountai to sōma, tō d᾽ heterō podi lithon perilabousai kratousi; synechei gar ho tēs haphēs tonos en tō mē katheudein polyn chronon. Hotan de anōsin, ekpesōn ho lithos tachy diēgeire tēn proemenēn]. Those that keep watch at night support the body on one of their legs, and hold a pebble grasped in the other foot. The effort of gripping holds off sleep for some time. But as soon as they relax, the falling stone at once wakes the negligent one. Aelian [III, 13.]: Ἑστᾶσι μὲν ἀσκωλιάζουσαι, τῷ γε μὲν μετεώρῳ ποδὶ λίθον κατέχουσι τοῖς ὄνυξι μάλα ἐγκρατῶς τε καὶ εὐλαβῶς· ἵνα ἐάν ποτε λάθωσιν ἑαυτὰς εἰς ὕπνον ὑπολισθαίνουσαι, πεσὼν καὶ ὑποκτυπήσας ὁ λίθος, ἀποδαρθάνειν καταναγκάσῃ [Hestasi men askōliazousai, tō ge men meteōrō podi lithon katechousi tois onyxi mala enkratōs te kai eulabōs; hina ean pote lathōsin heautas eis hypnon hypolisthainousai, pesōn kai hypoktypēsas ho lithos, apodarthanein katanankasē]. They rest on one foot only, and in the other, which is raised, they hold a pebble [II, 626] with their claws very firmly and with the greatest care, so that, if sleep should ever steal upon them, the falling pebble may wake them with its noise. Philes and Tzetzes say the same. Accordingly, when Aelian says that cranes swallow pebbles ὡς ἔχειν καὶ δεῖπνον, καὶ πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν ἀνέμων ἕρμα [hōs echein kai deipnon, kai pros tas embolas tōn anemōn herma], so as to have them both for a meal and as ballast against the onslaught of the winds, one should consider whether instead of δεῖπνον [deipnon] we ought to read δι᾽ ὕπνον [di᾽ hypnon], on account of sleep. For that pebbles should serve cranes as a meal is quite absurd. But perhaps Aelian meant that stones are swallowed by cranes not only to serve as ballast when they are about to fly across the Pontus, but also so that, once the sea has been crossed, they may be vomited up and serve to ward off sleep in the manner we have described.
